text: Everything from READ UNCOMMITTED through SERIALIZABLE is pessimistic -- it assumes conflicts are likely and uses locks to physically block other sessions. SNAPSHOT isolation throws that out entirely and uses row versioning instead: a consistent, point-in-time copy of the data as it looked when the transaction started.
First, it has to be turned on at the database level -- ALTER DATABASE, SET ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON. That's a one-time setup step, not something each session does.

Once that's on, a session sets SNAPSHOT isolation the same way as any other level. From that point, every read in the transaction sees the data exactly as it looked at the moment the transaction started, no matter what anyone else commits while it's running.

Because a SNAPSHOT read comes from a versioned copy rather than the live row, it never needs to wait on another session's lock -- and a writer never needs to wait on a SNAPSHOT reader either, because there's no shared lock there to wait on. Readers don't block writers, and writers don't block readers.

There's one conflict row versioning can't avoid: two SNAPSHOT transactions both trying to write the same row, based on the same starting snapshot. SQL Server detects this and raises error 3960 on the second one to commit -- it refuses to silently let a write overwrite data based on a stale snapshot.

Next lesson, a related but different idea: RCSI, Read Committed Snapshot Isolation, which uses this same row-versioning trick but changes what plain READ COMMITTED itself means, database-wide. See you there.
